replications.original_title: Creating brand names with meaning: the use of sound symbolism
replications.description: Study 1, H1a: Brand names with front (vs. back) vowels are perceived as smaller (tested with laptop computer category)
replications.explanation: Hypothesis supported: chi-squared = 49.09, p < 0.001, with 512 choosing front vowel sounds vs. 311 choosing back vowel sounds, in the predicted direction. Replication r = 0.244 vs. original r = 0.623.

replications.original_authors: Shrum, L. J.; Lowrey, Tina M.; Luna, David; Lerman, Dawn B.; Liu, Min
replications.original_title: Sound symbolism effects across languages: implications for global brand names
replications.original_journal: International Journal of Research in Marketing
replications.description: Experiments 1a, 1b, 1c: Front (back) vowel words are preferred for convertible/knife (4x4 vehicles/hammer), demonstrating sound symbolism effects on product name preferences across languages
replications.explanation: The authors state: 'Thus, we successfully replicated the previous findings.' A significant vowel x product category interaction was found (F(1,821) = 55.002, p < 0.001), with effects in the predicted directions for both product categories.

replications.original_title: Color saturation increases perceived product size
replications.description: Study 3: High (vs. low) color saturation increases product size estimates, with attention and arousal as mediators
replications.explanation: The main DV (size estimate) showed no effect: F(1,821) = 0.095, p = 0.758, replication r = 0.011 vs. original r = 0.295. The authors note: 'Given that our main result (i.e., saturation and size estimates) was not significant, we did not perform pre-registered mediation analyses.'

replications.original_title: Healthy-left, unhealthy-right: can displaying healthy items to the left (vs. right) of unhealthy items nudge healthier choices?
replications.description: Study 1B: Participants tend to prefer the healthy item (broccoli salad) when it is displayed on the left (vs. right) of unhealthy items
replications.explanation: The authors report: 'the frequency of choosing healthy food did not differ regardless of whether it was on the left (24.44%) or the right (25.59%) of the unhealthy food (chi-squared = 0.091, p = 0.763).' The replication effect size was r = -0.011 vs. original r = 0.241.

replications.original_title: A sound idea: phonetic effects of brand names on consumer judgments
replications.description: Study 1: Brand names including back (vs. front) vowels are rated as higher in the attribute perception index (richness, smoothness, and creaminess), with diagnosticity and timing as moderators
replications.explanation: The main effect of sound symbolism on the attribute perception index was significant (F(1,821) = 7.492, p = 0.006) but the predicted two-way and three-way interactions were not (p = 0.731 and p = 0.305). The brand evaluation index showed no main effect (p = 0.736). The authors describe this as a partial replication: 'partially replicated one of them (Yorkston and Menon, 2004).'

replications.original_title: The "visual depiction effect" in advertising: facilitating embodied mental simulation through product orientation
replications.description: Study 4: Visual product depictions within advertisements oriented toward a participant's dominant hand facilitate purchase intention through embodied mental simulation
replications.explanation: The authors report: 'The results of the analysis did not reveal any effects on purchase intentions (match: M = 3.39 vs. mismatch: M = 3.36; F(1,821) = 0.068, p = 0.794).' The replication effect size was r = 0.009 vs. original r = 0.400. The mediator (mental simulation) also showed no effect (p = 0.941).

replications.original_authors: Jiang, Yuwei; Gorn, Gerald J.; Galli, Maria; Chattopadhyay, Amitava
replications.original_title: Does your company have the right logo? How and why circular- and angular-logo shapes influence brand attribute judgments
replications.description: Experiment 1: Circular and angular-logo shapes influence consumers' judgment of softness-related and hardness-related product attributes (comfortableness and durability)
replications.explanation: The authors report: 'The results of the analysis did not reveal logo shape-by-cut attribute interactions (F(2,820) = 0.141, p = 0.868).' Individual comparisons also showed no effects on comfort (p = 0.949) or durability (p = 0.994). Replication r = 0.013 vs. original r = 0.251.

replications.original_title: The future looks "right": effects of the horizontal location of advertising images on product attitude
replications.description: Study 2: When participants are primed to desire a modern product, they are more favorable when it appears on the right; when primed to desire an antique, they are more favorable when it appears on the left
replications.explanation: The authors report: 'post hoc analyses did not reveal any hypothetical findings. Antique priming did not influence product attitudes depending on position (p = 0.859). Modern priming did not influence product attitudes depending on position (p = 0.405).' Replication interaction r = 0.061 vs. original r = 0.189.

replications.original_authors: Cian, Luca; Krishna, Aradhna; Elder, Ryan S.
replications.original_title: This logo moves me: dynamic imagery from static images
replications.description: Study 1: A logo that evokes greater perceived movement (logo dynamism) generates more favorable attitudes toward the brand
replications.explanation: The authors report: 'The results of the analysis did not reveal an effect on brand attitudes (high dynamism: M = 5.64 vs. low dynamism: M = 5.59; F(1,821) = 0.393, p = 0.531).' The manipulation check (perceived movement) was significant (p < 0.001), confirming the manipulation worked but the hypothesized effect on brand attitudes did not replicate. Replication r = 0.022 vs. original r = 0.261.

replications.original_authors: Madzharov, Adriana V.; Block, Lauren G.
replications.original_title: Effects of product unit image on consumption of snack foods
replications.description: Study 1A: Packages with more product units displayed on the package are perceived to contain more product quantity than packages with fewer product units displayed
replications.explanation: The authors report no effect on perceived product quantity (F(1,821) = 0.565, p = 0.452) or serving size (F(1,821) = 2.380, p = 0.123). A nonparametric test also did not reveal effects (U = 78,727, p = 0.081). Replication r for product quantity = 0.026 vs. original r = 0.407; replication r for serving size = 0.054 vs. original r = 0.348.
